stem: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) on Thursday retained Pakistan on its "Grey list" till June after concluding that Islamabad failed to _____ its strategically important deficiencies.

stem: A spring festival of Hindus, Ram Navami is celebrated to mark the birthday of Lord Rama, _____ is considered the seventh avatar of Lord Vishnu.
context: Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blanks :

stem: Chief Justice of India S. A. Bobde ______ office on April 23 after completing a tenure lasting 17 months.
context: Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blanks :
solution: 'Demit office' is the fixed formal expression for relinquishing a post at the end of a tenure, which is what a retiring Chief Justice does. Reassumed and joined both describe taking office rather than leaving it, and entitled does not take 'office' as an object at all. Matches option A.

stem: Despite knowing the health threats, many people ______ to quit the habit of smoking.
context: Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blanks :
solution: 'Despite knowing the health threats' sets up a contrast: knowing the risk has not produced the result you would expect, so the verb must describe continued failure. 'Struggle to quit' does exactly that. 'Manage to quit' is the trap - it means they succeed, which destroys the contrast the sentence is built on - and prepare and oppose do not fit 'to quit the habit'. Matches option B.

stem: Offering girls with education is a ____ step in developing future generations of healthy, educated, and empowering girls.
context: Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blanks :
solution: Educating girls is presented as the foundation on which healthier, better-educated later generations are built, so the adjective must mean first and most important: primary. Trivial says the opposite. Outstanding and influential rate how good or how powerful something is rather than placing it at the start of a process, and neither sits naturally with 'step in developing'. Matches option D.

stem: The animal rights movement and legal jurisprudence ____ that cruently is characterised by unacceptably high animal suffering.
context: Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blanks :
solution: The subject is compound - the movement and legal jurisprudence - so a present-tense verb must take the plural form. 'Claims' is the tempting choice on meaning but carries the singular ending and fails agreement. Among the remaining forms only 'state' can be followed by a that-clause: censor requires a direct object, and lauded is past tense and cannot govern 'that' in this construction. Matches option A.

stem: The CM ____ to migrant workers to not leave the city, stressing that the restrictions will be lifted as soon as possible.
context: Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blanks :
solution: One appeals to someone to do something, and that is exactly the pattern here: the Chief Minister asked migrant workers not to leave. stem: UK opposition leader demands Boris Govt to sanction telegram for ____ extremists.
context: Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blanks :
solution: To harbour extremists is to shelter them or give them refuge, which is the charge that would justify demanding sanctions against a platform. Debunking would mean exposing them, witnessing means only seeing, and yielding does not take people as its object here. Matches option A.

stem: The Egyptians were one of the first ____ to believe in an afterlife.
context: Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blanks :
solution: The Egyptians are being placed among the earliest societies to hold a belief, so the noun must name a society: civilizations. An administration is a government rather than a people, and conversations and impressions are not things that can believe in an afterlife. Matches option C.

stem: Tipu Sultan's historian Kate Brittlebank has ____ this painting on the cover page of her biography, Tiger: The Life of Tipu Sultan.

stem: While the information is somewhere in your long-term memory, you are not able to actually ____ and remember it.

stem: The deal ended after a series of ____ disputes.

stem: The first Islamic conquests of India ____ in the eleventh century, with the capture of Lahore, in 1021.

stem: Mayank was ____ by colleagues for leaking the confidential information on the rival company.
context: Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blanks :
solution: The blank sits inside a passive construction, so it needs a past participle, and 'criticized for' is the standard collocation when the fault is named. Reproach is printed in its base form and would have to be 'reproached' to fit at all, dissented is intransitive and cannot be made passive, and one is warned against doing something rather than warned for having done it. stem: The manager said to Shradha, "I can no longer tolerate your coming late."
optA: The manager advised Shradha that he should no longer tolerate her coming late.
optB: The manager asked Shradha if he could no longer tolerate her coming late.
optC: The manager warned Shradha that he could no longer tolerate her coming late.
optD: The manager told Shradha that he will no longer tolerate her coming late.
context: In the following questions, a sentence has been given in Direct or Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect or Direct speech.
solution: The remark is a reprimand about repeated lateness, so 'warned' is the reporting verb that fits. In indirect speech after a past reporting verb, 'can' backshifts to 'could' and 'your' becomes 'her'. The version using 'advised' wrongly substitutes 'should', the version using 'asked ... if' turns a statement into a question, and the remaining version leaves 'will' standing although the original modal is 'can'. Matches option C.

stem: Socrates said, "An unexamined life is not worth living."
optA: Socrates said that an unexamined life was not worth living.
optB: Socrates said that an unexamined life cannot be worth living.
optC: Socrates said that an unexamined life has not worth living.
optD: Socrates said that an unexamined life is not worth living.
context: In the following questions, a sentence has been given in Direct or Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect or Direct speech.
solution: 'An unexamined life is not worth living' is a general maxim rather than a report of something happening at one moment, and the rule for universal truths and proverbs is that the present tense is retained even after a past reporting verb. The other two versions are simply not English: 'has not worth living' is ungrammatical, and 'cannot be worth living' both alters the modality and fails to backshift. Matches option D.

stem: Sam said to me, "It has been raining for five hours."
optA: Sam told me that it had been raining for five hours.
optB: Sam told me that it was being raining for five hours.
optC: Sam told me that it is being raining for five hours.
optD: Sam told me that it might be raining for five hours.
context: In the following questions, a sentence has been given in Direct or Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect or Direct speech.
solution: The present perfect continuous of the direct speech, 'has been raining', moves back one step to the past perfect continuous, 'had been raining', after the past reporting verb 'told'. 'Was being raining' and 'is being raining' are not possible verb forms in English, and 'might be raining' turns a statement of fact into a guess. Matches option A.

stem: Maid said to his owner, "I will not come."
optA: Maid told his owner that he may not come.
optB: Maid told his owner that he should not come.
optC: Maid told his owner that he would not come.
optD: Maid told his owner that he will not come.
context: In the following questions, a sentence has been given in Direct or Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect or Direct speech.
solution: 'Will' backshifts to 'would' when the reporting verb is in the past, and the first-person pronoun of the direct speech becomes 'he'. 'May' and 'should' replace a flat refusal with permission and advice respectively, and leaving 'will' unchanged ignores the backshift altogether. Matches option C.

stem: Sandhya said, "My grandfather is sleeping now."
optA: Sandhya said that her grandfather was sleeping then.
optB: Sandhya said that her grandfather must be sleeping now.
optC: Sandhya said that her grandfather was being sleeping then.
optD: Sandhya said that her grandfather would be sleeping then.
context: In the following questions, a sentence has been given in Direct or Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect or Direct speech.
solution: Two changes are required: the present continuous 'is sleeping' becomes 'was sleeping', and the time adverb 'now' becomes 'then'. 'Was being sleeping' is not a possible form, 'would be sleeping' converts a statement into a prediction, and the version with 'must be sleeping now' both keeps 'now' unchanged and adds a supposition the speaker never made. Matches option A.

optA: Best Costume Design for La La Land
optB: Best Supporting Actor for Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them
optC: Best Supporting Actor for La La Land
optD: Best Costume Design for "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them"
solution: The passage opens on the costume prize: Mary Zophres was expected to win for her retro-revival clothes in La La Land, and the sentence then names Colleen Atwood as 'the eventual winner ... for Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them'. The two acting options can be discarded at once, and the passage never pairs Atwood with La La Land; that is the film she beat. Matches option D.

context: In each of the following questions, choose the word which is most similar in meaning to the given word.

Reason (R): The east of Western Ghats is on the lee side.

optB: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

solution: Moisture-laden south-west monsoon winds strike the windward western slopes of the Western Ghats, rise, cool and shed their rain there. By the time the air descends the eastern slopes it has lost its moisture and is warming, so it absorbs water rather than releasing it. The country east of the Ghats therefore lies in a rain shadow, and being on the lee side is precisely why its rainfall is scanty. Both statements are true and the second is the correct explanation of the first. Matches option A.

stem:
A person near point is 50 cm and his far point is 3 m . Power of lens he required for
(i) Reading (ii) For Viewing distinct stars
solution: Two separate corrections are needed. For reading, the eye must cope with an object at the normal near point of 25 cm, so the lens has to throw a virtual image of it out at this person's own near point of 50 cm. With \(u = -25\) cm and \(v = -50\) cm, \(1/f = 1/v - 1/u = -1/50 + 1/25 = 1/50\), giving \(f = +50\) cm and a power of \(+2\) dioptre, a converging lens. For distant stars the eye cannot focus beyond its far point of 3 m, so the lens must bring an object at infinity to an image at 3 m in front of the eye: with \(v = -3\) m and \(u\) infinite, \(f = -3\) m and the power is \(-1/3\), about \(-0.33\) dioptre, a diverging lens. Matches option C.

stem: Two mirrors are kept at \(60^{\circ}\) to each other. then number of images formed by them is
solution: For two plane mirrors inclined at an angle \(\theta\), first compute \(360^{\circ}/\theta\). Here \(360/60 = 6\), which is an even whole number, and in that case the number of images is one less than the quotient, so five images are formed. The rule differs when the quotient is an odd whole number, where the number of images equals the quotient itself, which is the usual source of confusion. Matches option A.
subject: Physics

stem: The distance of an object from a spherical mirror is equal to the focal length of mirror. Then image:
solution: The phrase spherical mirror covers both the concave and the convex case, and the two behave quite differently. For a concave mirror an object at the focus sends out a parallel reflected beam, so the image forms at infinity. For a convex mirror, placing the object a distance equal to the focal length in front gives \(1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/f + 1/f = 2/f\), so the image is virtual and sits only \(f/2\) behind the mirror, nowhere near infinity. Since one case gives infinity and the other does not, the image may be at infinity but is not obliged to be. Matches option B.
subject: Physics

Since one of the two cases gives infinity and the other does not, 'must be at infinity' (A) is false and 'must be at focus' (C) is false, and 'may be at infinity' (B) is exactly right. Worth flagging that testing only the concave case - the default reading of 'mirror' - makes A look correct; the convex case is the discriminating test point and it is the one the option wording is built around.]

stem: An object is placed in front of a spherical mirror whose 2 times magnified image is formed on screen. Then choose correct option.
solution: An image that can be caught on a screen is a real image, and a convex mirror can never form a real image of a real object, so the mirror must be concave. Any real image formed by a mirror is inverted, and by the sign convention the magnification is negative whenever the image is inverted. The magnification is therefore \(-2\) rather than \(+2\); a positive value of \(+2\) would describe the erect virtual image seen when the object sits inside the focus, which no screen can catch. Matches option B.

stem: The refracting angle of prism is \(60^{\circ}\) and minimum deviation of \(30^{\circ}\), then angle of incidence
solution: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, so the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence and the angle of incidence is half the sum of the refracting angle and the minimum deviation. Here that gives \((60^{\circ} + 30^{\circ})/2 = 45^{\circ}\). Matches option B.

stem: The wavelength of X-rays is of the order
solution: X-rays occupy the band of the electromagnetic spectrum between ultraviolet and gamma rays, with wavelengths running from about \(10^{-8}\) m down to \(10^{-11}\) m. That is precisely why they diffract from crystal lattices, whose atomic spacings are of the same order. One angstrom is \(10^{-10}\) m and sits squarely in that band, whereas a micrometre lies in the infrared and a centimetre and a metre are microwave and radio wavelengths. Matches option B.
subject: Physics

stem: Displacement current goes through the gap between the plates of a capacitor when the charge on the capacitor
solution: Maxwell's displacement current in the gap is \(I_d = \varepsilon_0 \, d\Phi_E/dt\), and since the field between the plates is fixed by the charge on them, this reduces to \(dQ/dt\). What matters is only that the charge is changing, not the direction in which it changes: a decreasing charge gives a displacement current one way and an increasing charge gives one the other way, and neither is zero. Each of the three conditions listed therefore does produce a displacement current, so the choice that accepts all of them is the complete one. Naming only the general condition is tempting, but it is not the fullest correct answer when the two special cases are separately offered and separately true. Matches option D.

stem: A concave mirror forms an enlarged, erect, virtual image of an object, only when the object is placed
optD: Between focus and centre of curvature
solution: The concave mirror produces a virtual image only when the reflected rays diverge, and that happens when the object lies nearer the mirror than the focus. In that position the image appears behind the mirror, erect and magnified, which is how a shaving or make-up mirror works. An object exactly at the focus sends out a parallel beam and forms no image at any finite distance, while an object at or beyond the centre of curvature gives a real, inverted image that a screen can catch. Matches option B.

stem: An under water swimmer cannot see very clearly even in absolutely clear water because of
optC: Reduction of speed of light in water
optD: Change in the focal length of eye lens
solution: Most of the eye's converging power comes from the front surface of the cornea, because the jump in refractive index from air at 1.00 to cornea at about 1.376 is large. Under water the air is replaced by water at 1.33, the index step almost vanishes, and the cornea loses nearly all its refracting power, so the effective focal length of the eye's optical system grows and light is brought to a focus behind the retina. The blur is therefore a focusing failure, not an absorption or scattering effect, which is exactly why swimming goggles restore an air gap in front of the cornea and with it sharp vision. Matches option D.
subject: Physics

stem: Incident angle of a ray of light is \(30^{\circ}\). The angle between incident and reflected ray will be
solution: Angles of incidence and reflection are both measured from the normal, and the law of reflection makes them equal, so the reflected ray also leaves at \(30^{\circ}\) from the normal. The incident and reflected rays lie on opposite sides of the normal, so the angle between the two rays is \(30^{\circ} + 30^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}\). Reading the angle from the surface instead of from the normal is the usual slip and would give the wrong pairing here. Matches option B.
subject: Physics

stem: The electromagnetic wave having the shortest wavelength is
solution: Running down the electromagnetic spectrum from long wavelength to short gives radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Gamma rays sit at the extreme short-wavelength, high-frequency, high-energy end, with wavelengths below about \(10^{-11}\) m, and radio waves at the opposite extreme with wavelengths from centimetres to kilometres. Matches option B.
subject: Physics

stem: If the far point of an eye is at 4 m then the eye is
solution: The normal eye can focus objects all the way out to infinity. An eye whose far point has come in to 4 m cannot focus anything beyond that, which is short sight, or myopia. The correcting lens must take an object at infinity and form its image at the far point, so with \(v = -4\) m and \(u\) infinite the focal length is \(f = -4\) m and the power is \(-1/4\), that is \(-0.25\) dioptre. The lens is diverging and the power is negative; a myopic eye is never corrected by a converging lens. No printed option carries \(-0.25\) dioptre, so the question cannot be answered exactly as it stands.

stem: The temperature which has same numerical value on Celsius and Fahrenheit scale is
solution: Set the two readings equal and call that common number \(x\). The conversion between the scales gives \(x = \frac{9}{5}x + 32\), so \(x - 1.8x = 32\), hence \(-0.8x = 32\) and \(x = -40\). Checking, \(-40\) degrees Celsius really is \(-40\) degrees Fahrenheit, the single point where the two scales cross. The value 273 belongs to the Celsius-to-Kelvin offset and has nothing to do with this pair of scales. Matches option C.

stem: The increase the length of brass rod by 2%, its temperature should increase by (\(\alpha = 0.00002\ ^{0}C^{- 1}\))
solution: Linear thermal expansion gives \(\Delta L / L = \alpha \, \Delta T\). An increase of 2 per cent means \(\Delta L / L = 0.02\), so \(\Delta T = 0.02 / 0.00002 = 1000\). The temperature must therefore rise by \(1000\) degrees Celsius. Reading 2 per cent as 2 rather than 0.02 is the usual error and would inflate the answer a hundredfold. Matches option C.

stem: If \(\lambda_{m}\) Denotes the wavelength at which the radiative emission from a black body at a temperature T K is Maximum, then
solution: Wien's displacement law states that the wavelength at which a black body radiates most strongly is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature, \(\lambda_m T = b\) with \(b\) about \(2.9 \times 10^{-3}\) m K. Hence \(\lambda_m \propto T^{-1}\). This is why a heated body glows dull red when moderately hot and shifts through orange and yellow towards blue-white as it gets hotter: the peak moves to shorter wavelength as the temperature rises. Direct proportionality would predict exactly the opposite shift, and independence would mean the colour never changed with temperature at all. Matches option B.

stem: The rate of cooling at 600 K , If surrounding temperature is 300 K is H . The rate of Cooling at 900 K is
solution: The body is hundreds of degrees above its surroundings, so Newton's law of cooling, which holds only for small temperature excesses, does not apply and Stefan's law must be used instead: the net rate of radiative loss goes as \(T^4 - T_0^4\). At 600 K the factor is \(600^4 - 300^4 = 300^4(2^4 - 1) = 15 \times 300^4\), and this rate is given the name \(H\). At 900 K the factor is \(900^4 - 300^4 = 300^4(3^4 - 1) = 80 \times 300^4\). The ratio of the two is \(80/15 = 16/3\), so the rate of cooling at 900 K is \(\frac{16}{3}H\). Matches option A.

stem: If a gas has \(n\) degrees of freedom ratio of specific heats of gas
solution: By the equipartition theorem each degree of freedom contributes \(\frac{1}{2}R\) per mole to the molar heat capacity at constant volume, so \(C_V = \frac{n}{2}R\), and for an ideal gas \(C_P = C_V + R = \left(\frac{n}{2} + 1\right)R\). Dividing gives \(\gamma = C_P/C_V = 1 + \frac{2}{n}\). Checking against known gases confirms it: a monatomic gas with three degrees of freedom gives \(1 + 2/3 = 1.67\) and a diatomic gas with five gives \(1 + 2/5 = 1.4\), both correct. Matches option D.
subject: Physics

stem: The triple point of water is
solution: The triple point of water is the single temperature and pressure at which ice, liquid water and water vapour coexist in equilibrium. It is fixed by definition at 273.16 K, equivalent to \(0.01\) degrees Celsius, and it long served as the defining fixed point of the kelvin. The tempting misreading is to attach the same number 273.16 to the Celsius scale, but on that scale the corresponding value is 0.01, not 273.16. Matches option B.

stem: Which of the following halide is most reactive towards \(S_{N}1\) reaction?
solution: The rate-determining step of an \(S_{N}1\) reaction is the ionisation of the carbon-halogen bond to give a carbocation, so the reaction is fastest for whichever halide forms the most stable cation. Carbocation stability runs tertiary above secondary above primary above methyl, because alkyl groups release electron density into the empty orbital by induction and hyperconjugation. Tertiary butyl bromide therefore ionises fastest; methyl bromide, which would have to form the very unstable methyl cation, is the slowest of the four by this route. Matches option A.

stem: Which of the following pairs, both are nucleophiles?
solution: The nucleophile is electron-rich and donates a lone pair; the electrophile is electron-poor and accepts one. The cyanide ion carries a negative charge with a lone pair on carbon, and ammonia carries a lone pair on nitrogen, so both members of that pair are nucleophiles. Boron trifluoride, boron trichloride and aluminium chloride are all electron-deficient with incomplete octets, and the bromonium and nitronium cations are positively charged, so every other pair contains at least one electrophile. Matches option B.

stem: IUPAC Name of oxalic acid is:
solution: Oxalic acid is \(HOOC-COOH\), a two-carbon chain carrying a carboxyl group at each end. The parent chain of two carbons is ethane, and two carboxyl groups make it a dioic acid, so the systematic name is ethanedioic acid, written with locants as ethane-1,2-dioic acid. Ethanoic acid is the single-carboxyl acetic acid and methanoic acid is formic acid, neither of which is a diacid at all. Matches option B.

stem: The acid which does not undergo HVZ reaction is:
solution: The Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction halogenates a carboxylic acid at the carbon next to the carboxyl group, working through the enol of the intermediate acid halide. That requires an alpha carbon bearing at least one hydrogen. Formic acid is \(HCOOH\): its carboxyl carbon is bonded only to a hydrogen and a hydroxyl group, so there is no alpha carbon at all and the reaction simply cannot begin. Acetic, propanoic and 2-methylpropanoic acids each have alpha hydrogens and all react normally. Matches option B.

stem: Urotropine is formed by the action of ammonia on:
solution: Urotropine, or hexamethylenetetramine, is the cage compound \((CH_{2})_{6}N_{4}\) formed when formaldehyde condenses with ammonia, six molecules of the aldehyde to four of ammonia with the loss of six molecules of water. It is used as a urinary antiseptic and as the fuel in solid camping tablets. Acetaldehyde with ammonia gives an aldehyde-ammonia adduct instead, and acetone and phenol give quite different products. Matches option B.

stem: Which of the following has the highest melting point?
optD: All have the same melting point
solution: All three isomers share the same molecular formula and have very similar boiling points, so the difference must lie in how well the molecules pack in the solid. The para isomer is symmetrical, so its molecules stack into a compact, well-ordered lattice that takes considerably more energy to break down; it melts at about 53 degrees Celsius, whereas the unsymmetrical ortho and meta isomers pack poorly and melt below room temperature. Symmetry raising the melting point sharply while barely affecting the boiling point is the general rule for such isomer sets. Matches option C.

stem: Which one of the following alkane is not formed in Wurtz reaction?
solution: In the Wurtz reaction two molecules of an alkyl halide couple through sodium metal, \(2R-X + 2Na \rightarrow R-R + 2NaX\), so the product always contains at least twice the carbon count of the smallest alkyl fragment. Ethane comes from methyl halide and butane from ethyl halide, and propane can be obtained as one product of a mixed coupling of methyl and ethyl halides. Methane has only a single carbon and cannot be assembled by joining two alkyl fragments together, so it is the one alkane this reaction can never yield. Matches option B.

stem: The correct order of acidic strength of carboxylic acid is:
optB: Formic acid < acetic acid < benzoic acid
optC: Acetic acid < benzoic acid < formic acid
optD: Acetic acid < formic acid < benzoic acid
solution: Compare the acids by how well each stabilises the anion it leaves behind. Formic acid carries only a hydrogen on the carboxyl carbon, with no electron-releasing group to destabilise the anion, and is the strongest of the three with \(pK_{a}\) about 3.75. Benzoic acid follows at about 4.20, since the ring withdraws electron density relative to an alkyl group. Acetic acid is the weakest at about 4.76, because the methyl group pushes electron density onto the carboxylate and destabilises it. Increasing acid strength therefore runs acetic, then benzoic, then formic. Matches option C.

stem: Aspirin is :
solution: Aspirin is made by acetylating the phenolic hydroxyl of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride, a step that leaves the carboxyl group untouched. The product is 2-acetoxybenzoic acid, universally called acetylsalicylic acid. Methyl salicylate is oil of wintergreen and phenyl salicylate is salol, and both of those are esters of the carboxyl group rather than acetylated phenols, which is what makes them tempting but wrong. Matches option C.

stem: Deficiency of Vitamin B causes:
solution: Beri-beri is the classic deficiency disease of thiamine, vitamin \(B_{1}\), and shows itself as nerve damage and heart failure. It appeared in populations living on polished rice, because milling strips away the thiamine-rich husk. Rickets instead follows a shortage of calciferol, the sunshine vitamin, and scurvy a shortage of ascorbic acid, so neither of those belongs to the thiamine group at all. Matches option D.

stem: \(S_{N}\ ^{1}\) reaction will be fastest in which of the following solvents?
solution: The slow step of an \(S_{N}1\) reaction is ionisation into a carbocation and a halide ion, so the solvent must stabilise separated charges. Polar protic solvents do this best: a high dielectric constant screens the two ions from each other, and the hydroxyl hydrogen bonds to and solvates the departing halide. Methanol is protic and has the highest dielectric constant of the four at 32, so it accelerates the reaction most. Acetone is comparably polar but has no hydroxyl to hydrogen bond to the leaving group, ethanol is protic but less polar, and chloroform at 5 is far too weakly polar to support ionisation at all. Matches option C.

stem: \(S_{N}1\) reaction of alky1 haldies leads to :
solution: The intermediate in an \(S_{N}1\) reaction is a carbocation, whose three bonds lie in a plane with an empty orbital perpendicular to it. The nucleophile can attack that flat centre from either face with roughly equal ease, so a single enantiomer of the starting halide yields nearly equal amounts of both product enantiomers and the optical activity is largely lost. Complete inversion is instead the signature of the concerted \(S_{N}2\) route, where the nucleophile is forced to attack from the side opposite the leaving group. Matches option B.

stem: The deficiency of which Vitamin causes rickets?
solution: Rickets is the childhood disease in which growing bone fails to mineralise properly, giving soft, bowed legs and swollen joints. It follows a shortage of calciferol, the fat-soluble sunshine vitamin, which is required for the absorption of calcium and phosphate from the gut and is manufactured in skin exposed to sunlight; that is why the disease was common among children in smoky industrial cities. Matches option D.

stem: Vitamin \(B_{2}\) is known as
solution: Vitamin \(B_{2}\) is riboflavin, named for its ribose-derived side chain and its yellow flavin ring system, and it is the precursor of the coenzymes FMN and FAD. The distractors are all genuine members of the same family under their own numbers: thiamine is vitamin \(B_{1}\), nicotinamide belongs to vitamin \(B_{3}\), and pyridoxine is vitamin \(B_{6}\). Matches option A.

stem: Sucrose on hydrolysis gives:
solution: Sucrose is a disaccharide in which the anomeric carbons of both units are locked into the glycosidic link, so hydrolysis by dilute acid or by invertase splits it cleanly into its two monosaccharides. The glucose unit is joined in the alpha configuration and the fructose unit in the beta configuration, so the products are \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and \(\beta\)-D-fructose. Because the mixture rotates plane-polarised light the opposite way from sucrose itself, it is known as invert sugar. Matches option D.

stem: The halogenated acid which does not obey Markownikoff's rule in presence of a peroxide is:
solution: The peroxide or Kharasch effect operates only with hydrogen bromide. The peroxide starts a radical chain by generating a bromine radical, which adds to the alkene so as to give the more stable carbon radical, leaving the hydrogen on the more substituted carbon and making the overall addition anti-Markownikoff. For hydrogen chloride the hydrogen-chlorine bond is too strong for the abstraction step to proceed, and for hydrogen iodide the iodine radical adds too reversibly to sustain a chain, so neither can propagate; the hydrogen-fluorine bond is stronger still. Matches option B.

stem: The carboxylic functional group \(( - COOH)\) is present in :
solution: Aspirin is 2-acetoxybenzoic acid: acetylation converts the phenolic hydroxyl of salicylic acid into an ester and leaves the \(-COOH\) group intact, which is why aspirin is still an acid and why it irritates the stomach lining. The other three are acidic without being carboxylic acids at all. Picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, acidic through a phenol group made strongly so by three nitro groups; barbituric acid is a cyclic imide; and ascorbic acid is a lactone whose acidity comes from an enediol hydroxyl. The name is the trap in each case. Matches option D.

stem: Mars is called the red planet because of the presence of large amount of
solution: The Martian surface is blanketed in fine dust rich in iron oxides, essentially rust, which reflects red wavelengths strongly and absorbs the blue, giving the planet its colour. Global dust storms keep the material suspended in the thin atmosphere, so even the Martian sky takes on a butterscotch tinge. Matches option B.

stem: Which planet of solar system has maximum number of satellites?
solution: Counting confirmed natural satellites, Saturn now leads the solar system with roughly 146, ahead of Jupiter at about 95. Most of Saturn's are small irregular bodies captured into distant, steeply inclined orbits and detected only in recent deep surveys. Jupiter is the tempting answer because it held the record for decades and is by far the largest planet, but the survey work of the last few years has put Saturn clearly ahead, while Uranus and Neptune trail with fewer than thirty each. Matches option A.

stem: Chlorophyll molecules are located in the
solution: Chlorophyll is a lipid-soluble pigment anchored in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast, held within the light-harvesting protein complexes of photosystem I and photosystem II. That location is essential rather than incidental: the membrane is the barrier across which the proton gradient driving ATP synthesis is built, so the pigment must sit in it. The stroma holds the enzymes of the dark reaction and the thylakoid lumen accumulates the protons, but neither holds the pigment. Matches option A.

stem:
Light reaction or photochemical phase includes
I. light absorption
II. water splitting
III. oxygen release
IV. ATP and NADPH formation
Select the correct option
solution: The light or photochemical phase covers everything driven directly by absorbed photons. The pigments absorb light, water is split at photosystem II, the oxygen given off comes from that splitting, and the electron flow that follows generates ATP and NADPH. All four listed items therefore belong to this phase, and only the fixation of carbon dioxide into sugar is left to the dark reaction. Matches option D.

stem: Which of the following organisms are capable of performing photosynthesis?
solution: Photosynthesis requires chlorophyll, and all three groups listed have it. Algae are photosynthetic, green plants are the obvious case, and insectivorous plants such as the pitcher plant and the sundew are fully green and manufacture their own food in the ordinary way. They trap insects not for energy but for nitrogen and other minerals, which are scarce in the waterlogged, acidic soils where they grow. Matches option D.
subject: Biology

stem:
Enzymes required in dark reaction are present in
______ of chloroplast.
solution: The dark reaction, or Calvin cycle, is a sequence of enzyme-catalysed steps beginning with RuBisCO fixing carbon dioxide onto a five-carbon sugar, and those enzymes are dissolved in the stroma, the fluid that fills the chloroplast around the thylakoids. Thylakoids, grana and lamellae are all names for parts of the membrane system, which is where the light reaction happens instead. Matches option C.

stem: The end products of photosynthesis in plants are
solution: Write the overall reaction as it is set out for green plants: \(6CO_{2} + 12H_{2}O \rightarrow C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2} + 6H_{2}O\). Reading off the right-hand side gives glucose, oxygen and water as the products. Starch is tempting, and plants certainly do accumulate it, but starch is formed afterwards by polymerising the glucose for storage, so it is a storage product rather than a direct end product of the pathway; that choice also omits the water entirely. Matches option D.
subject: Biology

stem: In the process of photosynthesis,
optC: water is oxidized and \({CO}_{2}\) is reduced
optD: water is reduced and \({CO}_{2}\) is oxidized.
solution: Photosynthesis is at bottom a redox process. Water is the electron donor: it is split at photosystem II, gives up electrons and hydrogen, and is thereby oxidised to molecular oxygen. Carbon dioxide is the electron acceptor: it takes up hydrogen carried by NADPH during the Calvin cycle and is thereby reduced to carbohydrate. Reversing the pairing would describe respiration releasing energy rather than photosynthesis storing it. Matches option C.

stem: Five-Kingdom classification was given
solution: R. H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom system in 1969, dividing living things into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia on the criteria of cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships. It displaced the older two-kingdom division into plants and animals associated with Linnaeus. Haeckel had earlier added Protista as a third kingdom, and Morgan worked on inheritance in fruit flies rather than on classification at all. Matches option B.

stem: Which among the following produce seeds?
solution: Seed formation is the defining innovation of the spermatophytes. Thallophyta, the algae, Bryophyta, the mosses and liverworts, and Pteridophyta, the ferns and horsetails, all reproduce by spores and still need a film of water for the male gamete to swim to the egg. Gymnosperms bear naked seeds on cones, with no ovary enclosing them, and are the first group in this list to make seeds at all. Matches option D.

stem: 'Ozone-hole' means
optA: a large sized hole in the ozone layer
optC: small holes scattered in the ozone layer
solution: The ozone hole is not a gap in the sense of a physical opening. It is a seasonal thinning, a sharp fall in the ozone column over Antarctica each spring, caused by chlorine radicals released from chlorofluorocarbons destroying ozone catalytically on the surfaces of polar stratospheric cloud particles. The layer remains continuous throughout; it is only far less dense than it should be, which is why the word hole is a metaphor rather than a description. Matches option B.

stem: Which of the following is not a general pollutant of atmosphere?
solution: The oxides of sulphur and nitrogen listed here are all injurious gases released mainly by burning sulphur-bearing fuel and by high-temperature combustion, and together they drive acid rain. Carbon dioxide is different in kind: it is a normal constituent of clean air at roughly 0.04 per cent, it is required for photosynthesis, and it is not counted among the ordinary air pollutants in this classification, even though its rising concentration matters greatly for the greenhouse effect. Matches option A.

stem: Phenomenon involving increase in concentration of non-degradable pollutants from lower to higher trophic levels is called.
solution: Bioaccumulation and biomagnification are easily confused and the stem is worded to separate them. Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a substance inside a single organism over its lifetime, because intake outpaces excretion. Biomagnification is the further concentration of a persistent, non-degradable substance at each successive trophic level, since a predator consumes many contaminated prey; this is how DDT concentrations climb from water to plankton to fish to fish-eating birds. The stem specifies an increase from lower to higher trophic levels, which is magnification rather than mere accumulation. Matches option A.
